Findings come from fixed review rules applied to the supplied inputs and to general literature; no experiment, simulation or independent review was performed.

checks.literatureReview: Not performed: Astroflare cites a curated list and does not search the literature.

derived.label: Total cabin pressure in kPa
assumptions: Unit conversion factor is exact; precision follows the supplied value.

derived.label: Oxygen fraction minus Earth-air reference
assumptions: Reference: dry air, 20.95% oxygen by volume.
For a difference, the result keeps the decimal places of the supplied value (1).
limitations: Says how far the oxygen fraction is from Earth air; says nothing about flammability by itself.

derived.label: Oxygen partial pressure
assumptions: Ideal-gas mixture: partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
Percent by volume is taken as mole fraction.
limitations: Flammability depends on oxygen fraction as well as partial pressure; this number alone does not rank two atmospheres.

derived.label: Oxygen partial pressure relative to Earth sea-level air
assumptions: Reference p(O2) = 21.23 kPa (sea-level air).
limitations: A ratio of conditions, not a risk measure.

derived.label: Nominal circuit power
assumptions: Steady operating values; no fault.
limitations: Not the power released in a fault or arc, which depends on fault impedance and arc behaviour.

derived.label: Let-through energy of the fault (I²t)
assumptions: The prospective fault current is constant for the whole clearing time.
Millisecond-to-second conversion is exact (÷1000).
limitations: Ignores arc voltage, current limiting and conductor heating.
NOT compared with any ignition limit: the cited methodology reports thresholds that are specific to the materials and wire configurations tested, and Astroflare holds none.

derived.label: Air turnover time of the compartment
assumptions: Well-mixed compartment.
limitations: A transport time scale only; it does not predict smoke concentration, detector response or flame behaviour.

derived.label: Minimum round-trip communication time
assumptions: Symmetric one-way delay; no processing or queueing time.
limitations: A lower bound: the earliest a ground reply could arrive.

findings.title: Plausible pathway: electrical overheating or arcing igniting insulation or nearby material
findings.statement: Electrical faults and wire-insulation combustion are described in the cited literature as a recognised ignition pathway in spacecraft. For the circuit described here this is a plausible pathway only; the inputs do not demonstrate that it can occur or that it cannot.
findings.reasoning: The sources describe wire insulation combustion as a likely cause of spacecraft fires, report Apollo-era work on wiring malfunction and current-overload flammability, and name electrical wiring among the most probable ignition sources in the Apollo 1 fire.
findings.relevance: Defines the hazard pathway under investigation.
limitations: The sources are general (drop-tower experiments, a 1971 paper, accident history). None characterises the circuit, materials or atmosphere described here.
A plausible pathway is not a measured failure rate or a prediction.

findings.title: Nominal circuit power
findings.statement: At 28 V and 12 A the circuit's nominal power is 3.4 × 10² W.
findings.reasoning: P = V × I (units V·A = W, checked).
findings.relevance: Context for the energy available to a fault.
limitations: Not the power released in a fault or arc.

findings.title: Let-through energy of the fault was calculated but cannot be compared with an ignition limit
findings.statement: With a prospective fault current of 150 A cleared in 5 ms, I²t = 1 × 10² A²·s. Astroflare holds no ignition thresholds, so this value is not judged high or low.
findings.reasoning: The cited NASA test methodology seeks ignition energy-density thresholds expressed through I²t values for specific materials and wires, and names oxygen pressure, wire diameter, heat sinking and contained smoke volume among the factors needed to relate such thresholds to a real design.
findings.relevance: Shows what additional data would turn this number into an ignition assessment.
limitations: The cited thresholds are specific to the materials and configurations tested and are not available to Astroflare.
The assumptions listed with the calculation apply.

findings.title: Fault protection is not demonstrated
findings.statement: Fault protection is specified but not tested. A specified protection is a proposed mitigation, not demonstrated performance.
findings.reasoning: Inference from the supplied input: how fast and how reliably a fault is cleared determines the let-through energy, which cannot be known without test data.
findings.relevance: Bears on how much energy a fault could deliver.
limitations: No source is cited for this statement.

findings.title: Ability to remove power is not verified
findings.statement: The procedure to remove power from the affected equipment is defined but not verified.
findings.reasoning: The ISS response sequence in the technical brief includes manually removing electrical power from hardware in the affected module to cease continuous ignition sources.
findings.relevance: An electrical ignition source can persist while the circuit remains energised.
limitations: The ISS sequence is an example, not a requirement for this design.

findings.title: Redundancy and emergency power are not fully defined
findings.statement: Redundancy and emergency power are partly defined, so the consequences of de-energising the circuit for other functions are not known.
findings.reasoning: Inference from the supplied input; no source is cited.
findings.relevance: De-energising may be impractical if it removes essential functions.
limitations: Significance is not quantified.

findings.title: No documented inspection history
findings.statement: Inspection and maintenance history is not documented, so the condition of wiring and connections cannot be assessed.
findings.reasoning: Inference from the supplied input; no source is cited.
findings.relevance: Condition affects fault likelihood, which Astroflare does not estimate.

findings.title: Oxygen fraction is about equal to Earth air
findings.statement: The supplied oxygen fraction is 21.0% by volume, equal to Earth air within ±0.1 percentage points (reference 20.95%). The total pressure gives an oxygen partial pressure of 21.3 kPa, 1.00 times that of sea-level Earth air. This does not establish that Earth-based material data apply: total pressure and gravity may also differ.
findings.reasoning: Direct comparison with the reference value.
findings.relevance: Context for choosing applicable material data.
limitations: A lower oxygen fraction does not by itself imply a lower hazard; other conditions are unchanged by this comparison.

findings.title: Reduced-gravity fire and smoke behaviour differs from Earth-based expectations
findings.statement: Gravity regime supplied: Microgravity. Literature cited here reports that without buoyancy flames and smoke behave differently from normal gravity, and that fire-safety design has often relied on 1 g understanding.
findings.reasoning: Cited sources report that without buoyancy flames burn equally in all directions, that thin-sheet materials show reduced flammability and flame spread in quiescent low gravity, that smoke particles can grow larger in low gravity, and that detectors were designed on normal-gravity data.
findings.relevance: Determines which test data, detector designs and flame-spread assumptions can be transferred.
limitations: Several statements concern thin-sheet fuels or older experiments; they are not tests of this scenario.
Large-scale reduced-gravity fire data are limited (see limitations).

findings.title: Material flammability evidence is incomplete
findings.statement: Material flammability evidence is partial.
findings.reasoning: The technical brief states material flammability must be assessed in the relevant cabin atmospheres and gravity levels; the interim standard in the library defines flammability test methods (its current revision must be checked).
findings.relevance: Material data apply only to the conditions tested.
limitations: Which materials, atmospheres and gravity levels were tested was not supplied.

findings.title: Ability to stop ventilation is not verified
findings.statement: Ventilation to the affected compartment is reported as stoppable, but this is not reported as verified. A proposed capability is not evidence that it works.
findings.reasoning: The ISS response sequence in the technical brief includes terminating ventilation in the affected module; whether it works here is not shown by the inputs.
findings.relevance: Determines whether the response step can be relied on.
limitations: Verification status is as reported by the user; Astroflare cannot check it.

findings.title: Air turnover time scale of the compartment
findings.statement: With 30 m³ and 20 m³/min the compartment air turns over in 2 minutes (volume ÷ flow).
findings.reasoning: Arithmetic on supplied values.
findings.relevance: Gives a transport time scale for comparing with detector response and response times.
limitations: Does not predict smoke concentration or detector response; assumes a well-mixed compartment.

findings.title: Detection coverage is limited
findings.statement: Detection coverage is one zone or one detector. Time to detection depends on where detectors are relative to a fire.
findings.reasoning: The technical brief states detection depends on knowing where detectors should be located and the associated time to detection.
findings.relevance: Bears on how quickly an event would be noticed.
limitations: No detector performance data were supplied.

findings.title: Fire signatures detected are limited
findings.statement: Detection is supplied as smoke/particulate only.
findings.reasoning: Cited sources state fire emissions depend on fuel type, heating conditions, gravity and atmosphere, that detectors must handle a wide variety of fires, and that spacecraft smoke detectors were designed on normal-gravity data.
findings.relevance: Inference from the cited statement that emissions depend on heating conditions: overheating insulation may produce different emissions from a flaming fire. Which signatures appear first in this scenario is not established by the inputs.
limitations: No emission data for the materials in this scenario were supplied.

findings.title: No combustion-gas monitoring supplied
findings.statement: Combustion-gas monitoring is not part of the detection supplied. The cited brief describes carbon monoxide buildup as an additional early-warning source.
findings.reasoning: The technical brief states buildup of atmospheric gases, particularly carbon monoxide, is an additional early-warning source and that ISS uses continuous atmospheric sampling; an instrument paper describes combustion-product monitoring for early warning and post-fire clean-up.
findings.relevance: Gas monitoring also informs post-fire clean-up.
limitations: The sources describe capability, not whether it is needed for this design.

findings.title: Suppression provisions are limited
findings.statement: Suppression is portable extinguishers only. Adequacy for this hazard (for example energised electrical equipment, access behind panels) is not assessed.
findings.reasoning: The technical brief states extinguishing equipment must be usable in microgravity, accessible, and must not create additional hazards, and that automated systems are needed where crews cannot extinguish a fire.
findings.relevance: Bears on whether a detected event could be controlled.
limitations: No agent, quantity or access information was supplied.

findings.title: Crew breathing protection is not confirmed as accessible
findings.statement: Crew breathing protection is available but access is not verified.
findings.reasoning: The technical brief states protective equipment must be donned in smoke or near a fire because even small concentrations of some combustion products can be immediately harmful.
findings.relevance: Bears on crew exposure during response.
limitations: Verification status is as reported by the user.

findings.title: Post-fire monitoring and clean-up plan is incomplete
findings.statement: The post-fire monitoring and clean-up plan is partial.
findings.reasoning: The technical brief states considerable clean-up is required after all fire events, the state of the environment to be scrubbed must be specified, and the crew must be able to determine whether the atmosphere is safe enough to remove breathing apparatus.
findings.relevance: Combustion products can remain after flames are out.
limitations: No contaminant levels or limits were supplied.

findings.title: Limited return or safe-haven options
findings.statement: Return or safe-haven options are not available quickly.
findings.reasoning: Inference: response would then rely on the vehicle's own resources. The technical brief lists no emergency resupply, limited stowage of suppressant and diluents, and delayed ground communications among deep-space challenges, and states current ISS solutions are not designed for long-duration missions.
findings.relevance: Bears on how much of the response must be self-contained.
limitations: The brief describes challenges, not a quantified consequence for this scenario.

findings.title: Mission duration
findings.statement: Mission duration supplied: 180 days. The cited roadmap paper lists extended duration among factors that expand the fire-safety parameter space but gives no duration threshold, so Astroflare does not classify this duration as extended or not.
findings.reasoning: Direct restatement with a pointer to the cited roadmap statement.
findings.relevance: Context.
limitations: Duration alone does not change any finding.

findings.title: Communication delay with the ground
findings.statement: With a one-way delay of 12 minutes, the earliest possible ground reply is 24 minutes after a message is sent, so ground consultation cannot be part of any response step shorter than that.
findings.reasoning: Round-trip time is twice the one-way delay (arithmetic). The technical brief also notes ground consultation may be of poor quality and delayed.
findings.relevance: Shows which decisions must be made on board.
limitations: A lower bound; real delays include processing and queueing.

findings.title: Large-scale reduced-gravity fire data are limited
findings.statement: Cited NASA work states that the lack of experimental data at practical length scales and geometries has forced designers to rely on 1 g understanding, and that fire spread and growth cannot be expected to scale linearly.
findings.reasoning: Applies to every fire-related finding in this report.
findings.relevance: Limits how far any statement here can be extrapolated to a real vehicle.
limitations: The statements come from abstracts of Saffire experiment papers.

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Fire Protection (OCHMO-TB-008, Rev A)
sources.issuer: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer (OCHMO)
caveats: The brief states it is derived from NASA-STD-3001, is for reference only, and does not supersede or waive Agency, Program or Contract requirements.
Much of it describes International Space Station practice; statements about deep-space missions are described as challenges and open gaps, not solutions.
Requirement numbers (for example [V2 9059]) appear as quoted in the brief; NASA-STD-3001 itself was not reviewed.

review.note: All 16 pages were read from the PDF text on 2026-10-21.

verification.detail: The link answered; the document content was not re-read.

claims.text: For the Apollo 1 fire (1967), an unidentified ignition event led to rapid fire spread in the closed cabin; electric wiring and plumbing carrying a combustible coolant were considered the most probable ignition sources.

The ISS fire response sequence includes detection and warning, terminating ventilation in the affected module to slow the spread of fire, donning protective masks, manually removing electrical power from hardware in the affected module to cease continuous ignition sources, and then using fire extinguishers.

Changes in gravity and airflow alter how fire behaves. Without buoyancy, flames burn equally in all directions, and ventilation fans can supply the air a fire needs so that fire can spread in any direction.

Material flammability must be assessed in relevant cabin atmospheres and gravity levels for exploration transit vehicles and habitats, and design requirements need to specify the permitted combinations of pressure and oxygen percentage in the habitable volume.

Human-crew spacecraft require automated detectors that respond to fire signatures (temperature rise, combustion gases, light and other radiation, particulates, pressure rise, acoustic waves); rapid detection with limited false alarms is needed, and detection depends on knowing where detectors should be located and the associated time to detection.

Buildup of atmospheric gases, particularly carbon monoxide, is an additional source of early warning of a fire; the ISS uses continuous atmospheric sampling that can detect carbon monoxide buildup as confirmation of a fire.

Extinguishing equipment must be usable in microgravity without assistance from gravity, clearly identified and accessible, and must not create additional hazards; protective equipment must be donned in smoke or near a fire because even small concentrations of some combustion products can be immediately harmful.
Automated systems are to be used where crews are not capable of extinguishing fires, including large fires, fires where the crew could be absent, and fires in volumes inaccessible to the crew.

Considerable clean-up is required after all fire events; the state of the environment to be scrubbed (pressure, temperature, composition) must be specified, the crew must be able to determine whether the atmosphere is safe enough to remove breathing apparatus, and the ventilation system may need to be shut down to protect the crew.

For deep-space missions the brief lists no emergency resupply, more limited stowage of suppressant and atmospheric diluents, and consultation and emergency communications with the ground that may be of poor quality and delayed; it states the technical solutions currently implemented on the ISS are not designed for long-duration missions.
In space smoke does not rise, so smoke detectors are placed within the ventilation system; airflow must be provided in occupied areas to make smoke visible or detectable by odour.

The ISS fire response sequence includes detection and warning, terminating ventilation in the affected module to slow the spread of fire, donning protective masks, manually removing electrical power from hardware in the affected module to cease continuous ignition sources, and then using fire extinguishers.

Changes in gravity and airflow alter how fire behaves. Without buoyancy, flames burn equally in all directions, and ventilation fans can supply the air a fire needs so that fire can spread in any direction.
Experiments in spacecraft and drop towers show that thin-sheet materials have reduced flammability ranges and flame-spread rates in quiescent low gravity compared with normal gravity.
Owing to the absence of microgravity smoke data, all spacecraft smoke detectors current at the time were designed on normal-gravity conditions.

Removing buoyancy reduces velocities in the high-temperature zones of flames, increasing the residence time of smoke particles and allowing longer particle growth; shuttle experiments confirmed larger particle sizes in some cases.

The lack of experimental data at practical length scales and geometries has forced spacecraft designers to base designs and safety precautions on 1-g understanding of flame spread, flame self-extinguishment, fire detection and suppression; the Saffire experiments address this.

Material flammability must be assessed in relevant cabin atmospheres and gravity levels for exploration transit vehicles and habitats, and design requirements need to specify the permitted combinations of pressure and oxygen percentage in the habitable volume.

This interim standard establishes requirements, criteria and test methods for evaluating the flammability, offgassing and compatibility of materials intended for space vehicles, ground support equipment and facilities.

Human-crew spacecraft require automated detectors that respond to fire signatures (temperature rise, combustion gases, light and other radiation, particulates, pressure rise, acoustic waves); rapid detection with limited false alarms is needed, and detection depends on knowing where detectors should be located and the associated time to detection.
Fire emissions are affected by fuel type, heating conditions, gravity and exploration atmosphere.
Effective spacecraft fire detectors must detect a wide variety of fires, and the authors recommend research toward detectors that selectively detect a broad variety of fires.

Buildup of atmospheric gases, particularly carbon monoxide, is an additional source of early warning of a fire; the ISS uses continuous atmospheric sampling that can detect carbon monoxide buildup as confirmation of a fire.

The Combustion Product Monitor is a six-channel tunable laser absorption spectrometer that measures gas-phase CO, HCl, HCN, HF, CO2 and O2 in spacecraft environments; the authors state that monitoring these compounds can provide early warning of combustion events and facilitate safe post-fire clean-up.

Extinguishing equipment must be usable in microgravity without assistance from gravity, clearly identified and accessible, and must not create additional hazards; protective equipment must be donned in smoke or near a fire because even small concentrations of some combustion products can be immediately harmful.
Automated systems are to be used where crews are not capable of extinguishing fires, including large fires, fires where the crew could be absent, and fires in volumes inaccessible to the crew.

Considerable clean-up is required after all fire events; the state of the environment to be scrubbed (pressure, temperature, composition) must be specified, the crew must be able to determine whether the atmosphere is safe enough to remove breathing apparatus, and the ventilation system may need to be shut down to protect the crew.

For deep-space missions the brief lists no emergency resupply, more limited stowage of suppressant and atmospheric diluents, and consultation and emergency communications with the ground that may be of poor quality and delayed; it states the technical solutions currently implemented on the ISS are not designed for long-duration missions.

NASA states that past spaceflight operations covered a narrow range of conditions from a fire-safety perspective, and that missions beyond low Earth orbit expand the parameter space to include extended durations, dormancy intervals, increased oxygen concentrations, partial gravity and surface dust, each of which can significantly affect fire-safety system design and operations.

A large-scale fire was intentionally set inside a spacecraft in orbit for the first time; earlier low-gravity tests aboard spacecraft were limited to small samples, and fire spread and growth and their interaction with the vehicle cannot be expected to scale linearly.
In space smoke does not rise, so smoke detectors are placed within the ventilation system; airflow must be provided in occupied areas to make smoke visible or detectable by odour.
Adding a ventilating air flow to the low-gravity flame zone can greatly enhance the flammability range and flame spread.

tensions.note: Airflow can enhance flame spread by supplying a fire with air, which is why the ISS sequence terminates ventilation in the affected module; but smoke detection relies on airflow to bring smoke to detectors. Whether stopping ventilation is net beneficial depends on detector placement, flow rates and fuel, none of which these sources resolve for a specific design.

limitations: Astroflare has not been validated against experiments and has not been reviewed by a qualified safety authority. It is a screening and evidence-organising aid, not a safety determination.
No probability, frequency, severity, margin or confidence interval is estimated.

A low number of flagged conditions does not mean the spacecraft is safe, and a high number does not mean an incident is likely: flags reflect which conditions the rules recognise in the supplied inputs.
A proposed mitigation is not a demonstrated mitigation. Provisions are reported as the user described them and are not checked.
Cited statements are general. They are not tests of the design described and may be outdated or specific to conditions that differ from this scenario.
11 of the 12 cited sources were reviewed at abstract level only; their full text was not read.
Sources published 10 or more years ago: S03, S05, S02, S08, S12. Age says nothing about correctness, but conditions and methods may have changed.

Competing considerations (ventilation): Airflow can enhance flame spread by supplying a fire with air, which is why the ISS sequence terminates ventilation in the affected module; but smoke detection relies on airflow to bring smoke to detectors. Whether stopping ventilation is net beneficial depends on detector placement, flow rates and fuel, none of which these sources resolve for a specific design.

30 supplied inputs are the user's estimate or working assumption (Hazard under investigation; Habitat or vehicle; Mission phase; Gravity; Oxygen fraction; Total cabin pressure; Volume of the affected compartment; Ventilation flow through the compartment; Ability to stop ventilation to the affected compartment; Mission duration; Crew size; Return or safe-haven options; One-way communication delay to ground; Equipment type; Operating voltage; Operating current; Prospective fault current; Fault clearing time of the protective device; Fault protection; Procedure to remove power from the affected equipment; Redundancy and emergency power; Inspection and maintenance history; Fire detection coverage; Fire signatures detected; Fire suppression provisions; Crew breathing protection; Crew fire-response practice; Post-fire monitoring and clean-up; Material flammability evidence; Other ignition sources considered). Calculations and findings that use them are only as reliable as those estimates.
Provisions reported at their strongest level but supported only by an estimate or assumption, so they should be treated as unverified: Crew fire-response practice.

summary.text: Scenario: electrical overheating or arc. This is a preliminary screening of the inputs supplied, not a risk estimate. Screening result: 15 conditions warrant review and 0 information gaps limit the assessment. Conditions flagged: let-through energy of the fault was calculated but cannot be compared with an ignition limit; fault protection is not demonstrated; ability to remove power is not verified and 12 more. Most consequential unresolved issue: let-through energy of the fault was calculated but cannot be compared with an ignition limit (the order of items is presentational, not a ranking of risk). Evidence limitations: findings rest on general NASA literature, mostly reviewed at abstract level, not on tests of this design; no probability or severity is estimated and no independent validation has been performed. The hazard pathway is a plausible one drawn from the literature, not a demonstrated failure mode of this system.
